extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical geometry; readers of Euclid's Elements and mathematical historians
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of definitions, theorems and methodological comments from T. L. Heath's translation and notes on Euclid's Elements (Books III–V). Focuses on geometric definitions (circles, sectors, segments), propositions about chords/tangents/centres, and commentary about proof method and ratio definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.1 — Equal circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal circles are those the diameters of which are equal, or the radii of which are equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.2 — Tangent to a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line is said to touch a circle which, meeting the circle and being produced, does not cut the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classical Euclidean definition of a tangent (the note discusses internal vs external contact and the minimal admissions necessary for proofs such as III.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.3 — Circles touching one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Circles are said to touch one another which, meeting one another, do not cut one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers both internal and external contact; commentary notes that Euclid often proves the harder case and leaves the easier external case to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.4 — Equal distance from centre
rubrics_metrics.description: In a circle straight lines are said to be equally distant from the centre when the perpendiculars drawn to them from the centre are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'distance' of a straight line from the centre via perpendicular length; later propositions use this notion (Heron and later commentators compare alternate formulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.5 — Greater distance
rubrics_metrics.description: And that straight line is said to be at a greater distance on which the greater perpendicular falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.6 — Segment of a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: A segment of a circle is the figure contained by a straight line and a circumference of a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.7 — Angle of a segment
rubrics_metrics.description: An angle of a segment is that contained by a straight line and a circumference of a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath's note: historically interesting but Euclid rarely uses the notion; includes reference to 'angle of a semicircle' and 'horn-like angle' appearing in later propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.8 — Angle in a segment
rubrics_metrics.description: An angle in a segment is the angle which, when a point is taken on the circumference of the segment and straight lines are joined from it to the extremities of the straight line which is the base of the segment, is contained by the straight lines so joined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.9 — Angle stands upon a circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: And, when the straight lines containing the angle cut off a circumference, the angle is said to stand upon that circumference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.10 — Sector of a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: A sector of a circle is the figure which, when an angle constructed at the centre of the circle, is contained by the straight lines containing the angle and the circumference cut off by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholiast note: distinguishes sectors with vertex at centre from sector-like figures with vertex elsewhere; historical remarks on terminology (shoemaker's knife analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition III.11 — Similar segments of circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar segments of circles are those which admit equal angles, or in which the angles are equal to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan observes the use of 'similar' anticipates similarity of form; commentary notes this definition is essentially a theorem if 'similar' has its final meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proof to unnecessary reductio ad absurdum
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a direct demonstration is available, prefer it to a reductio ad absurdum that destroys multiple hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath (quoting De Morgan) points out that III.1's proof can be given directly and that the reductio form has the disadvantage of destroying two hypotheses; prefer direct proofs that avoid extraneous assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tacit/unproved assumptions in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any fact used in a proof that is not trivial should be proved explicitly rather than left tacit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath repeatedly flags tacit assumptions in Euclid's proofs (e.g. assumptions about where points fall relative to triangles in III.7–8) and recommends proving such subsidiary facts (De Morgan's corrections and suggested lemmas are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's methodological habit: prove the hardest case
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid often proves the more difficult or obscure case and leaves the simpler cases to the reader's intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentary notes this practice (e.g. III.6 internal contact is proven; external case left implicit); awareness of this habit is important when reading or writing classical-style proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Porism usage as short lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Porisms (short consequences) serve as reusable lemmas: e.g., if a straight line in a circle cuts another into two equal parts at right angles, the centre lies on the cutting line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath highlights such porisms (porism to III.1) and their use as auxiliary facts in subsequent propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use converses to illuminate relations and supply extra results
rubrics_metrics.description: Converse statements of Euclid's propositions are often true and can be proved (sometimes by reductio) to clarify geometric relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath recommends proving converses (e.g., converses of III.7 and III.8) to understand cases like internal contact and relative centre positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: At most two equal straight lines from a point to a line not through the point
rubrics_metrics.description: Not more than two equal straight lines can be drawn from a given point to a given straight line not passing through it—one on each side of the perpendicular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to prove things like a straight line cannot cut a circle in more than two points and to justify uniqueness claims in constructions (referenced proofs: use Produs on I.16 or I.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: A straight line cannot cut a circle in more than two points
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line cannot intersect a circle in more than two points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition III.10 establishes this; Heath notes the proof covers meeting or cutting (internal/external) and also discusses alternate demonstrations from earlier texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two circles that meet (cut or touch) cannot share the same centre unless they coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: If the circumferences of two circles meet at a point, the circles cannot have the same centre unless they coincide everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositions III.5–6 and commentary treat both cutting and touching (internal and external contact); Heath discusses subtle assumptions (e.g. that touching internally implies prior passage through interior points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of centre by equal chords
rubrics_metrics.description: If more than two equal straight lines fall from a point to a circle, that point is the centre of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition III.9 and its proofs (including Simson's alternative) show logical equivalence with parts of III.7; used as a diagnostic test for centrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-length criteria for lines from a point to a circle (III.7–8)
rubrics_metrics.description: From an internal point the line through the centre is greatest and the one opposite/produced through the centre is least; for external points the line through the centre is greatest on the concave circumference and the one between the point and the diameter is least on the convex circumference; nearer-to-centre/perpendicular criteria order other lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath records Euclid's formulation and alternative enunciations by H. M. Taylor, Nixon, and Heron, noting different choices of criteria (angle subtended at centre vs perpendicular-distance) and warning about unproved assumptions in Euclid's original proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential economy in definitions (minimize definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's practice is to keep definitions to the minimum necessary for later propositions, leaving other properties to be inferred when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath remarks that Euclid avoided striking out obsolete/traditional definitions (e.g. 'angle of a segment') but otherwise minimized definitional baggage; commentators sometimes propose alternative or supplemental definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid V.Def.5 — equal ratios via equimultiples
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's definition (Book V, Def. 5) defines equal ratios by comparing all equimultiples: two ratios are equal if for all natural multiples m,n we have m·A > n·B exactly when m·C > n·D, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath's lengthy note shows this definition matches Dedekind's modern conception of separating rationals into two classes and discusses alternative formulations proposed by later geometers (Saccheri, Fanfani, Ingenuo, Veronese).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for greater/less ratio using multiples; single counterexample suffices for disproportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid's test for one ratio being greater than another is the existence of equimultiples m,n with m·A > n·B while m·C ≤ n·D (and analogous tests); disproportionality can be established by a single counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath records Saccheri's remarks that a single instance can deny proportion (disproportion is simpler to detect); also notes omitted cases in Euclid's statement and how later authors supply full coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound ratio (V.Def.8–10) and duplicate/triplicate ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: The compound of ratios is the single ratio equivalent to successive alterations; duplicate, triplicate ratios are special cases (compound of equal ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Morgan's explanation treats 'compound ratio' as composition of successive alterations; Heath notes concerns about existence proofs (vi.12 required for some general claims) and historical use in problems like duplication of the cube.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical completeness: prove partial converses where useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a theorem's converse is relevant to geometric questions (e.g., internal contact and position of centres), it should be stated and proved to remove tacit inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath repeatedly suggests adding converses (or at least noting them) to clarify Euclid's development and to avoid hidden assumptions; converses can often be proved by reductio ad absurdum or by small auxiliary lemmas.
